minor_characters.name: Vivaldo
minor_characters.appearances_summary: A traveller present at the funeral of the shepherd Grisóstomo who converses with Don Quixote and hears Marcela’s defense (Ch 013).
minor_characters.reason_removable: He functions as a bystander and foil at the funeral scene and can be folded into a generic mourner without affecting the plot or themes.

minor_characters.name: Ambrosio
minor_characters.appearances_summary: Grisóstomo’s friend and priest who denounces Marcela and conducts the burial rites in the pastoral episode (Ch 012–014).
minor_characters.reason_removable: His specific identity is not essential; the funeral’s role in provoking Marcela’s speech can proceed with unnamed mourners.

minor_characters.name: Pedro (the goatherd)
minor_characters.appearances_summary: A talkative goatherd who hosts Don Quixote and Sancho, tells long set‑ups to the Marcela/Grisóstomo story, and mediates rustic scenes (Ch 011–012).
minor_characters.reason_removable: He primarily pads exposition and rustic colour; the pastoral episode can be reached more directly without him.

minor_characters.name: Antonio (the singing goatherd)
minor_characters.appearances_summary: Performs a long ballad ‘Antonio’s Ballad’ for the party among the goatherds (Ch 011).
minor_characters.reason_removable: A decorative performance that does not advance plot or character and may be cut wholesale.

minor_characters.name: Don Luis
minor_characters.appearances_summary: The disguised young ‘muleteer’ musician revealed as a noble runaway pursuing Doña Clara; creates a separate lovers’ thread at the inn (Ch 042–044, 046).
minor_characters.reason_removable: His aristocratic‑elopement thread is self‑contained and can be excised without touching the main Sierra Morena/inn convergence.

minor_characters.name: Doña Clara de Viedma
minor_characters.appearances_summary: The judge’s daughter and object of Don Luis’s pursuit at the inn (Ch 042–044, 046).
minor_characters.reason_removable: Her role is limited to the Don Luis subplot, which can be removed intact.

minor_characters.name: The Canon of Toledo
minor_characters.appearances_summary: Meets the party on the road; delivers a lengthy critique of books of chivalry and contemporary drama (Ch 047–048).
minor_characters.reason_removable: He serves as an essayistic mouthpiece; his presence and discourse can be omitted without affecting events.

minor_characters.name: Second Barber (original owner of the basin)
minor_characters.appearances_summary: Reappears to reclaim his ‘basin’ and provokes the pack‑saddle/helmet scuffle at the inn (Ch 045).
minor_characters.reason_removable: A reprise joke that can be compressed or cut; the Mambrino gag has already landed earlier.

minor_characters.name: Officers of the Holy Brotherhood (individuals)
minor_characters.appearances_summary: Arrive at the inn, brawl over the basin and pack‑saddle, and later escort Don Quixote’s ‘enchantment’ (Ch 045–046).
minor_characters.reason_removable: They can be reduced to nameless functionaries or elided; the staged ‘enchantment’ can proceed under the curate/barber alone.

minor_characters.name: Eugenio (the goatherd)
minor_characters.appearances_summary: Ch 050–051: Stops to tell the long framed tale of Leandra, Vicente de la Roca, and the lovesick shepherds of the Sierra Morena.
minor_characters.reason_removable: A self-contained inset story; none of its characters recur or affect Don Quixote or Sancho’s journey.

minor_characters.name: Leandra, Vicente de la Roca, and Anselmo
minor_characters.appearances_summary: Ch 051–052: Figures within Eugenio’s goatherd tale—Leandra elopes with Vicente, Anselmo and Eugenio lament; all remain within the framed narrative.
minor_characters.reason_removable: They exist only within the goatherd’s digression and never intersect the main cast again.

minor_characters.name: The Penitents and their clergy
minor_characters.appearances_summary: Ch 052: A confraternity procession encounters Don Quixote; a scuffle ensues before misunderstandings are cleared.
minor_characters.reason_removable: A one‑off roadside melee that contributes neither to the Duke–Duchess prank arc nor to Sancho’s governance arc.

minor_characters.name: Academicians of Argamasilla (mock epitaph writers)
minor_characters.appearances_summary: Ch 052: Provide satiric epitaphs and sonnets at the close of Part I.
minor_characters.reason_removable: Meta-parodic curtain call with no plot consequence; cutting it does not affect comprehension of Part II.

minor_characters.name: Don Lorenzo de Miranda
minor_characters.appearances_summary: Ch 068–070: Don Diego’s poet son exchanges poems and literary talk with Don Quixote.
minor_characters.reason_removable: A pleasant side portrait that neither advances Don Quixote’s Saragossa aims nor the Carrasco/Duke–Duchess throughline.

minor_characters.name: Don Juan and Don Jeronimo
minor_characters.appearances_summary: Ch 099–101: Two gentlemen at an inn who read from the spurious Second Part and chat with Don Quixote.
minor_characters.reason_removable: An early metatextual nod that duplicates later, more important denouncements in Seville; trimming avoids redundancy.

minor_characters.name: The landlord, cook, and kitchen staff at the ‘cow-heel’ inn
minor_characters.appearances_summary: Ch 099–101: Provide comic business with Sancho over supper and the scarcity of hens.
minor_characters.reason_removable: Local color only; excising the scene preserves all main arcs and character beats.

minor_characters.name: The Shepherdesses and their brother
minor_characters.appearances_summary: Ch 058: A costumed pastoral troupe invite Don Quixote to dine; shortly after, a drove of bulls tramples through.
minor_characters.reason_removable: A detachable pastoral interlude whose characters do not return and whose outcome does not redirect the plot.

minor_characters.name: The ‘Cart of Death’ players and Master of the ceremonies
minor_characters.appearances_summary: Ch 063: Traveling players dressed as allegorical figures brawl with Don Quixote in passing.
minor_characters.reason_removable: A throwaway scuffle with strangers that has no later resonance given the preserved Master Pedro puppet episode.

minor_characters.name: Claudia Jerónima
minor_characters.appearances_summary: Ch 112: a high‑spirited young woman who shoots her faithless lover Don Vicente and then resolves to enter a convent, met while Don Quixote is with the bandit Roque Guinart.
minor_characters.reason_removable: Her tragic one‑chapter tale is self‑contained and does not affect Quixote’s or Sancho’s arc or the Barcelona through‑line.

minor_characters.name: Don Vicente Torrellas
minor_characters.appearances_summary: Ch 112: Claudia Jerónima’s lover whom she mortally wounds; dies in her arms.
minor_characters.reason_removable: He exists only to complete Claudia’s side story, which is orthogonal to the main plot.

minor_characters.name: Doña Guiomar de Quiñones
minor_characters.appearances_summary: Ch 112: a regent’s wife briefly detained and then courteously released by Roque’s band.
minor_characters.reason_removable: This cameo serves only to showcase Roque’s ‘magnanimity’ and can be omitted without loss.

minor_characters.name: Two Spanish captains of infantry
minor_characters.appearances_summary: Ch 112: stopped and assessed by Roque’s band, then released on payment.
minor_characters.reason_removable: They are one‑scene foils in the Roque interlude and not needed for the core narrative.

minor_characters.name: Pilgrims to Rome
minor_characters.appearances_summary: Ch 112: briefly detained by Roque and then gifted coin.
minor_characters.reason_removable: They contribute nothing to the arcs or themes beyond padding the Roque episode.

minor_characters.name: Gascon squire punished by Roque
minor_characters.appearances_summary: Ch 112: a bandit who grumbles about Roque’s generosity and is struck down by him.
minor_characters.reason_removable: His only function is to underline Roque’s severity within a removable subplot.

minor_characters.name: Castilian advice‑giver in Barcelona
minor_characters.appearances_summary: Ch 114: heckles Don Quixote in the street during Don Antonio’s prank parade.
minor_characters.reason_removable: A one‑scene scold whose removal does not change any outcome.

minor_characters.name: Don Pedro Noriz
minor_characters.appearances_summary: Ch 114: one of Don Antonio’s friends who quizzes the enchanted head.
minor_characters.reason_removable: Named solely to ask a question; the head’s exhibition works without him.

minor_characters.name: Italian translator of ‘Le Bagatelle’
minor_characters.appearances_summary: Ch 114: argues translation with Don Quixote in the Barcelona printing‑house.
minor_characters.reason_removable: A faceless stand‑in for a meta‑literary aside that can be cut wholesale.

minor_characters.name: Musician–poet at Altisidora’s bier
minor_characters.appearances_summary: Ch 121–122: sings stanzas and later chats about poetic licence during the ducal pageant.
minor_characters.reason_removable: He adorns the pageant but is not needed for the simple fact that Altisidora ‘dies and rises’ by a prank.

minor_characters.name: Rhadamanthus and Minos (pageant judges)
minor_characters.appearances_summary: Ch 121: named roles in the ducal court’s mock infernal ceremony demanding Sancho’s smacks and pinpricks.
minor_characters.reason_removable: Their mythic names add colour only; the jest works without specifying them.

minor_characters.name: Tosilos (the duke’s lacquey, roadside)
minor_characters.appearances_summary: Ch 118: meets Sancho on the road, shares wine and cheese, and recounts aftermath of the earlier mock duel.
minor_characters.reason_removable: A callback cameo that neither advances plot nor themes at this stage.

minor_characters.name: Viceroy of Barcelona
minor_characters.appearances_summary: Ch 115–116: receives Ana Félix and helps arrange Don Gregorio’s rescue.
minor_characters.reason_removable: His named presence can be collapsed into ‘the authorities’ without altering the Ana Félix/Ricote rescue beat the synopsis requires.

minor_characters.name: Valencian general of the galleys
minor_characters.appearances_summary: Ch 115–116: hosts Don Quixote aboard and captures the corsair brigantine.
minor_characters.reason_removable: He can be anonymized as ‘the galley commander’ or omitted in favour of a brief narrative summary of the rescue.

subplots.name: The Captive’s Tale (Ruy Pérez de Viedma and Zoraida)
subplots.reason_removable: A celebrated inset novella that does not alter the main Sierra Morena/inn arc; all core recognitions and the curate’s reading occur without it.

subplots.name: Don Luis and Doña Clara’s elopement thread
subplots.reason_removable: A parallel lovers’ diversion at the inn; excising it leaves the Dorotea/Fernando/Luscinda recognitions intact.

subplots.name: Return of Andrés (the flogged boy) to denounce Don Quixote
subplots.reason_removable: A callback that underlines Quixote’s misread ‘succours’ but adds little beyond repetition; the theme is already clear.

subplots.name: Basin and pack‑saddle rematch brawl
subplots.reason_removable: A reprise of the Mambrino joke that can be condensed or dropped without losing the running gag.

subplots.name: Antonio’s rustic ballad among the goatherds
subplots.reason_removable: A pleasant stopover that neither drives the plot nor reveals new facets of the principals.

subplots.name: The Goatherd’s Tale of Leandra
subplots.reason_removable: A framed novella that halts the journey; none of its conflicts or characters inform Don Quixote’s or Sancho’s later choices.

subplots.name: The Penitents’ ‘Battle’
subplots.reason_removable: A misadventure duplicating earlier ‘misrecognition’ fights; cutting it tightens the transition into Part II without loss.

subplots.name: The Enchanted Bark
subplots.reason_removable: A picturesque set‑piece that neither changes Don Quixote’s resolve nor Sancho’s skepticism, and has no later callbacks.

subplots.name: The Cart of Death pageant
subplots.reason_removable: Another roadside clash with itinerants; keeping Master Pedro’s puppet show covers the ‘players’ motif more centrally.

subplots.name: Pastoral Troupe and the Bulls
subplots.reason_removable: A brief Arcadia pastiche ending in a trampling; it does not alter goals or relationships and can be lifted cleanly.

subplots.name: Early salon on the spurious Second Part
subplots.reason_removable: Later, more consequential encounters (e.g., Seville and Don Álvaro Tarfe) cover this meta-thread; this earlier scene can be excised without loss.

subplots.name: Roque Guinart and the bandits (including Claudia Jerónima’s tragedy and the equitable division of spoils)
subplots.reason_removable: The entire bandit detour delays Barcelona and introduces a historical outlaw and side tales that do not bear on the main Barcelona–Moreno–galleys–White Moon arc.

subplots.name: Public promenade with a placard (‘This is Don Quixote of La Mancha’), boys’ furze prank, and street heckling
subplots.reason_removable: A house‑party prank and crowd scene that add ridicule but no plot turns the synopsis depends on.

subplots.name: Don Antonio’s late‑night ball and the two mischievous ladies who dance Don Quixote into exhaustion
subplots.reason_removable: An amusing interlude that can be removed without affecting the talking‑head episode or later events.

subplots.name: Sancho’s ‘flight without wings’ hazing on the galley benches
subplots.reason_removable: Comic business separable from the Ana Félix/Don Gregorio rescue which the synopsis specifies.

subplots.name: Village wager over a fat man racing a thin man ‘with equal weights,’ arbitrated by Sancho
subplots.reason_removable: A one‑off comic judgement that neither propels the journey home nor develops character beyond traits already well‑established.

subplots.name: Roadside lunch with Tosilos (duke’s lacquey) and his update on Doña Rodríguez’s suit
subplots.reason_removable: A backward‑looking callback to the ducal prank that can be elided in a tight through‑line.

subplots.name: The ‘bristly adventure’: a night stampede of six hundred pigs that tramples master and man
subplots.reason_removable: A slapstick mishap isolated from any consequential choice or outcome.

subplots.name: Hare‑and‑omens scene and cricket‑cage purchase at the village gate
subplots.reason_removable: A comic misreading of omens instantly undercut by Sancho that adds no needed beat to the homecoming.

digressions.reason_removable: A thematic essay that can be drastically shortened or cut without confusing events or character arcs.

digressions.topic: Canon’s critique of chivalric books and contemporary drama
digressions.reason_removable: Extended literary theory slows momentum; its points can be implied elsewhere or omitted entirely.

digressions.topic: Chrysostom’s poems (‘Lay of Despair’) and other long verses
digressions.reason_removable: The funeral and Marcela’s defense can stand without reproducing multiple lengthy lyric insertions.

digressions.topic: Inserted songs and versified interludes among the goatherds
digressions.reason_removable: Pastoral colour that can be trimmed with no loss to the plot or to Marcela’s core argument.

digressions.topic: Notice of the ‘Novel of Rinconete and Cortadillo’ found in a valise
digressions.reason_removable: A meta‑literary aside introducing another inset tale that is not pursued; safe to excise.

digressions.topic: The Canon’s critique of chivalric books and Don Quixote’s counter-arguments
digressions.reason_removable: Extended essayistic back‑and‑forth that restates themes already established, stalling the story’s close of Part I.

digressions.topic: Mock epitaphs and sonnets by the ‘Academicians of Argamasilla’
digressions.reason_removable: A meta-parodic coda with no narrative consequence; amusing but dispensable in an abridgment.

digressions.topic: Author’s preface and dedication to the Count of Lemos
digressions.reason_removable: Cervantes’ frontal meta-commentary on envy, age, and rival continuations; valuable contextually but extraneous to plot.

digressions.topic: Don Lorenzo’s poetics (acrostic ‘Dulcinea del Toboso’, sonnetry talk)
digressions.reason_removable: A literary colloquy that flatters Don Quixote’s wit but can be cut without affecting the travel or prank arcs.

digressions.topic: Don Quixote’s rhapsodic set-piece on knightly baths and bevy of damsels
digressions.reason_removable: A luxuriant fantasia nested in the canon debate; trimming it streamlines the transition to action.

digressions.topic: Barcelona printing‑house tour, theory of translation, and on‑the‑spot encounter with the spurious ‘Second Part’
digressions.reason_removable: A meta‑literary excursus that does not change the Barcelona arc or the later formal repudiation via Don Álvaro Tarfe’s notarial declaration.

digressions.topic: Philological aside on Arabic loan‑words in Spanish and the instrument ‘albogues’
digressions.reason_removable: A linguistic essaylet that neither advances plot nor reveals new interiority.

digressions.topic: Ekphrasis of the inn’s painted hangings (Helen’s rape; Dido and Aeneas) with Don Quixote’s commentary
digressions.reason_removable: Scene dressing and classical riffing that can be cut without affecting the journey or themes.

digressions.topic: Altisidora’s ‘vision’ of hell with devils playing tennis with books (satirizing the false sequel)
digressions.reason_removable: Redundant meta‑satire given the Tarfe declaration; the essential point—that Altisidora’s death and revival are a ducal prank—stands without it.
